title: Sardines Benefits: What One Can Does for Your Heart and Bones
meta_description: Sardines benefits in real numbers: the protein, calcium, vitamin D, omega-3 and sodium in one can, plus how sardines compare with canned salmon.
excerpt: What one can of sardines gives you for heart and bones, in real numbers: protein, calcium, vitamin D, omega-3s and the sodium to watch.
author: marcus
content:
A can of sardines is small. The label on the back is not. Most people asking about sardines benefits want one thing: what does this can actually give me? Here it is in real numbers, for your heart and your bones.

Short version first. One can gives you a full serving of fatty fish, with the calcium still in it. The one number to watch is sodium.

A can of fish is one piece of your day, not the whole plan. If you want to see where your own calories and protein land, run the free PescoDial calculator first.

What's in One Can of Sardines

Start with the size. USDA's standard can is 3.75 ounces, which drains down to about 92 grams of fish, a little over one 3-ounce serving. One can, one serving. No scale needed.

Here's what USDA FoodData Central lists for Atlantic sardines canned in oil, drained, with the bones in, per 3 ounces (85 grams):

What you getAmount in 3 ozWhy it matters
ProteinAbout 21 gramsWhat muscle is built from
CalciumAbout 325 mgAlmost all of your body's calcium is stored in bones and teeth
Vitamin DAbout 4 mcgHelps your body absorb calcium
Omega-3s (EPA plus DHA)About 0.8 gramsThe fats the heart guidance is built around
SodiumAbout 260 mgThe number to check on the label

Brands differ, so the label on your own can is the final word.

Sardines Benefits for Your Heart

The American Heart Association recommends 2 servings of fish a week, with a serving being 3 ounces cooked, and it points people toward fatty fish in particular. Sardines are on its list of fatty fish, so two cans a week fits that pattern.

Why fatty fish? Because of the omega-3 fats called EPA and DHA. Your body makes only very small amounts of them, so they mostly come from food, and they're found in fish and other seafood. Sardines sit in the same fatty-fish group as salmon, herring and Atlantic mackerel. Lean white fish carries far less: USDA lists about 0.1 gram in 3 ounces of cooked cod. The full comparison is in which fish are high in omega-3.

No single food does the job alone. Sardines are one useful piece of a heart-healthy pattern.

Sardines are also small fish. The FDA and EPA put them on the Best Choices list, the lowest-mercury group on their chart. For how many fish meals a week make sense at your age, see how much fish per week after 60.

The sodium line

Standard guidance is to keep the whole day under 2,300 mg of sodium. Put the sodium figure from the table next to that ceiling: about 260 mg is roughly 11% of the day.

Here's the protocol at the shelf:

  1. Flip the can over. Find the sodium line on the Nutrition Facts panel.
  2. Check the serving size. Some labels count the whole can, some count part of it.
  3. Compare two or three brands. Sauce can add salt. USDA's record for sardines in tomato sauce lists about 350 mg of sodium per 3 ounces, against about 260 mg for sardines in oil. "No salt added" on the front makes it simple.

If you take medicine: sardines are food, but a few medicines are worth a conversation before you change how much fish you eat. If you take a blood thinner such as warfarin, bring questions about eating more oily fish and omega-3s to your pharmacist, who knows your full medicine list. If you take blood-pressure medicine, the sodium in canned fish is the part to ask about. If you take a statin or diabetes medicine, a real change in what you eat can change your numbers, and your doctor will want to know about it. Any change to your medicine is your prescriber's decision. This is not for everyone. Talk to your doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart problems, diabetes, are pregnant, or take medicine.

Sardines Benefits for Your Bones

Here's the thing most people miss. The calcium is in the bones of the fish. In a can, those bones are soft enough to eat, and the NIH lists canned sardines and salmon with bones among the foods that contain calcium. USDA's canned pink salmon records show how much the bones matter: about 240 mg of calcium per 3 ounces for the regular kind, about 50 mg for the skinless, boneless kind. So if you buy boneless, skinless sardines, check the calcium line on the label.

The NIH lists the daily calcium need for women aged 51 and over as 1,200 mg. Compare that with the calcium line in the table above. One serving won't cover a day, but about 325 mg is roughly a quarter of it without a glass of milk.

Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium, and fatty fish is one of the few foods that naturally has any. The NIH lists the daily vitamin D need for adults up to age 70 as 15 mcg, so the 4 mcg in a serving of sardines is roughly a quarter of that. Sardines bring both nutrients in the same can.

Sardines vs Salmon

Stop overthinking it. Both are fatty fish, both are on the FDA and EPA's lowest-mercury list, and both count toward your fish servings for the week.

The fair comparison is can against can. Regular canned pink salmon, drained, has about 240 mg of calcium, 12 mcg of vitamin D and 0.9 grams of EPA plus DHA per 3 ounces. Line those up against the sardine table.

  • For calcium: the rule is the same for both. Bones in, calcium in. A fresh salmon fillet has no soft bones to eat.
  • For taste: salmon is milder. If sardines are too strong for you, canned salmon with bones is a similar package.

My answer: keep both in the cupboard. When I stock my mother's kitchen, canned salmon goes on the shelf because it's the one she likes, and the fish she'll actually eat beats the fish with the better label.

The Other Small Oily Fish: Anchovies and Mackerel

Anchovies. Small and oily, like sardines. The catch is salt. USDA lists five canned anchovy fillets at about 730 mg of sodium, far more than a full 3-ounce serving of sardines. People typically use them as a flavouring, a fillet or two at a time, not as the main serving.

Mackerel. The species matters here. The FDA and EPA list Atlantic mackerel as a Best Choice, and it's a fatty fish like sardines. King mackerel is a different fish and sits on the FDA's Choices to Avoid list, the group with the highest mercury levels. If a can or a menu just says "mackerel" and doesn't name the species, pick something else.

When to Talk to Your Doctor

Sardines are an ordinary food for most people. These signs are worth getting checked:

  • Home blood pressure readings that keep running above the target your doctor gave you
  • New swelling in your ankles or legs, or sudden weight gain over a few days
  • Unusual bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums if you take a blood thinner
  • A broken bone from a minor fall, or a noticeable loss of height
  • A joint that suddenly turns hot, swollen and painful

Chest pain or pressure, sudden shortness of breath, or swelling of the lips or throat, hives or trouble breathing after eating fish is an emergency. Call 911 or your local emergency number.

The Bottom Line

One can of sardines is one serving of fatty fish. It brings protein, omega-3s, calcium and vitamin D together, as long as you eat the bones. Two cans a week lines up with the heart guidance on fish. Read the sodium line before the can goes in the cart. Simple beats perfect.
